voice: Archaeological investigation in Upano began long before the recent headlines. Sangay was known as a major archaeological site from the 1970s. Excavations at Sangay and Kilamope uncovered household floors, holes for timber support posts, hearths and pottery. They showed that people had lived and worked at particular locations. However, a detailed excavation covers only a small part of the landscape. A trench can reveal soil layers while leaving a distant path or another settlement outside its view. It is like studying one room without seeing the surrounding neighborhood. Researchers therefore expanded their questions from individual earth mounds to the land between them. Was this land unused, or did it contain fields and routes that supported the settlements? In 2015, Ecuador's national heritage institute commissioned an airborne lidar survey. It created an opportunity to compare a much wider view with years of excavation and field research. Survey patterns could suggest connections, while work on the ground could test those interpretations. Local knowledge of paths, fields and changes in the ground also belongs in this account. The valley's history did not become real only when researchers published it. The technological change was the ability to examine extensive terrain systematically and relate many observations to one another.

voice: Lidar measures distances using laser light pulses and the time required for reflected light to return to the instrument. From an aircraft, it measures points on vegetation and ground surfaces. Many pulses strike leaves and branches. Some pass through openings between leaves and reach lower surfaces. The reflected signals from the ground are valuable, but they are not equally available everywhere. The laser does not make solid leaves transparent, and it does not photograph buried houses. The measurements form a three-dimensional set of points. Researchers process those points to distinguish likely ground measurements from reflections off vegetation and other objects. They then construct a terrain model, sometimes estimating the surface between sparse measurements. Lighting the model virtually from different directions can make low ridges and depressions easier to see. These displays still require interpretation. Roots, erosion, recent tracks and natural drainage may produce confusing shapes. A clear line on a screen is not sufficient proof of an ancient construction. In Upano, the new patterns could be compared with earthworks already examined through field research. The discovery therefore resulted from several methods working together. It was not a complete hidden city appearing when someone pressed a button.

A path helps explain a raised building base; the building base gains context from nearby cultivated land and drainage. Together these features reveal ways of organizing daily activity through the terrain. The spaces between buildings matter because food production, movement and water management occur there. Calling this urbanism opens a discussion of settlement and scale, without making Upano identical to societies with different materials and institutions. Contemporary communities and researchers are also part of the continuing investigation and care of archaeological places.
